titel: Regimini militantis Ecclesiae — the founding bull, with the Formula of the Institute
warum: The corpus's opening document: the bull of 27 September 1540 by which Paul III approved the ten companions' own sketch of their way of life — the Formula of the Institute, quoted whole inside the papal frame — and capped the Society at sixty members. The apparatus now opens and closes with the two papal documents that made and unmade the old Society.
quelle: Latin after Institutum Societatis Iesu, vol. I (Bullarium et compendium privilegiorum), Florence 1892, pp. 3–7; Internet Archive Institutum1, OCR emended against the sense. English: this site's unofficial working translation. The revised Formula of 1550 (Exposcit debitum) is named, not carried.

titel: Exhortations and instructions on the Institute (selections)
warum: The man Ignatius sent across Europe to explain the Exercises and the Institute to the Society itself — the first authorised interpreter.
quelle: Latin after the Monumenta Ignatiana, series secunda (Madrid, 1919; the same public-domain volume this apparatus uses for the Exercises and the Directory), which prints Nadal's annotations on the General Examen from his autograph. Shipped: the 'In Examen annotationes', in which Nadal reads the Society's vocation out of the Exercises and gives the phrase 'simul in actione contemplativus', with this site's working translation (CC0). The Apologia for the Exercises and the prayer instructions are the named next steps.

titel: Of Conformity to the Will of God — the Eighth Treatise
warum: Three centuries of Jesuit formation read this book; the school of discernment as a daily curriculum, and the direct ancestor of the Abandonment attributed to Caussade.
quelle: English after The Practice of Christian and Religious Perfection, vol. I (Dublin: James Duffy, 1861; US public domain) — made, as its title page states, not from the Spanish but from the French of the Abbé Régnier-Desmarais: the classic transmission chain of this book, carried as it stands. Shipped: the Eighth Treatise of the First Part, Of Conformity to the Will of God, complete in all thirty-four chapters. The Spanish original (Ejercicio de perfección, Seville 1609) is named as source but not yet carried.

warum: The school distilled to a single motion: the present moment as the sacrament of God's will. Written before the suppression, printed long after — the Favre pattern of transmission.
quelle: English after Ella J. McMahon's translation, Abandonment; or, Absolute Surrender to Divine Providence (New York: Benziger Brothers, 1887; US public domain). Carried whole as Ramière shaped the book in 1861: his doctrinal preface, the treatise in three books (9 + 12 + 12 chapters), and the appendix of pieces by other hands (Surin, Bossuet, Francis de Sales, the acts of abandonment, and La Colombière's act of confidence). The French original (ed. Ramière, Lyon 1861) is named as source but not yet carried. The attribution is debated in modern scholarship and is stated as debated.

warum: The pedagogical constitution of the order — the document that made Aristotle's De anima and Aquinas's Summa the curriculum of every Jesuit college, and so the hinge between the Constitutions and the school's doctrine of the soul.
quelle: Latin after the definitive Ratio atque Institutio Studiorum of 1599 as printed in the Institutum Societatis Iesu, vol. III (Florence, 1893; US public domain), collated where doubtful with Pachtler's edition of 1887 (Monumenta Germaniae Paedagogica V, which prints the 1599 text beside that of 1832). Carried complete and bilingual: the rules for the professor of scholastic theology (14 — rule 2 binds the schools to St. Thomas, with the Society's liberty stated in the same breath) and for the professor of philosophy (20 — rule 2 binds them to Aristotle, the De anima course following in the curriculum rules). The English is this site's working translation (CC0), without authority — cite the Latin.

titel: Commentarii in tres libros De anima — the Prooemium
warum: The science of the soul beneath the school of discernment: the De anima course of the Coimbra college, where the order worked out its doctrine of the senses, the imagination and the intellect — the anthropology the Exercises presuppose when they set the imagination to compose a place and the intellect to weigh an election.
quelle: Latin transcribed by eye from the page images of the 1617 printing (Internet Archive commentariicolle00col, columns 2–7); first printed Coimbra 1598; the modern editions are in copyright and were not used. Shipped: the Prooemium complete and bilingual — what the science of the soul is, its utility, its place in the physics course, the disputed subject of the three books, and their partition. The English is this site's working translation (CC0). Named next steps: the Prooemium's Quaestio unica and the internal-senses questions of book III.

titel: Commentaria in libros De anima — three chapters
warum: The order's greatest philosopher on the cooperation of the soul's powers — sense, imagination and intellect rooted in the same soul and working in harmony — the doctrine at work wherever the Exercises set imagination and intellect to prayer together.
quelle: Latin after the Vivès Opera omnia, vol. III (Paris 1856; US public domain; Internet Archive tomus-19-francisci-suarez), printing the posthumous text completed by Baltasar Álvares (Lyon 1621); the critical edition (Castellote, 1978–1991) is in copyright and was not used. Shipped complete and bilingual: II.3 (the powers flow from the soul and are rooted in it), III.30 (one interior sense, not four — the seven vocabula reduced to a single power), and IV.7 (the intellect in this life depends on the phantasy). The English is this site's working translation (CC0).

warum: The Exercises carried to the other side of the world within a decade of their approval.
quelle: English: H. J. Coleridge, The Life and Letters of St. Francis Xavier, 2 vols. (London 1872; Internet Archive lifelettersofstf01cole / lifelettersofstf02cole, public domain). Four letters carried complete — Cochin 1543, Kagoshima 1549, to Ignatius 1552, Sancian 1552 — cut at their printed openings and datelines, Coleridge's commentary and footnotes omitted. Latin originals: Monumenta Xaveriana (1899–1912), not yet carried.

titel: The Jesuit Relations from New France (selections)
warum: The order's world reporting: mission, ethnography, martyrdom — annual letters that became a genre. Le Jeune opens the wintering chapter with Epictetus; Brébeuf's Instructions are the canoe-borne mirror of Ricci's change of habit.
quelle: English after R. G. Thwaites's edition and translation, The Jesuit Relations and Allied Documents, 73 vols. (Cleveland: Burrows Brothers, 1896–1901; pre-1930, US public domain), via the Creighton University electronic transcription, spot-verified against the Internet Archive scans of the Burrows printing; Thwaites's page numbers are carried on every paragraph. Four selections in the genre's three registers: Le Jeune wintering with the Montagnais (Relation of 1634, ch. XII; JR 7), Brébeuf's Instructions for the Fathers who shall be sent to the Hurons (Relation of 1637; JR 12), and the capture of Saint-Ignace with the deaths of Brébeuf and Lalemant (Ragueneau, Relation of 1649; JR 34, chs. III–IV). The French originals stand on the facing pages of the same public-domain volumes, named but not yet carried.

titel: De Christiana expeditione apud Sinas — in Purchas his Pilgrimes (selections)
warum: Inculturation argued at the court of China: the boldest application of Ignatian adaptability — read here through the eyes of a Protestant compiler of 1625, a double transmission that is itself part of the story.
quelle: English after Samuel Purchas's digest of 1625 ('A Discourse of the Kingdome of China, taken out of Ricius and Trigautius', with the mission narrative and the death of Ricci), as reprinted by MacLehose (Hakluytus Posthumus, vol. XII, Glasgow 1906; US public domain twice over). Eight sections cut to the argument: the entry of Ruggieri and Ricci, the alteration of habit from bonze to literatus, Nanquin with the Booke of Friendship; the kingdom's name and greatness, its characters, studies and degrees, the three sects, the strangers and forraine religions; and the death of Ricci with Pantoja's petition for a burial place. Purchas's orthography kept as printed. The Latin original (Trigault, Augsburg 1615) is named as source but not yet carried; Gallagher's 1953 translation is in copyright and was not consulted.

titel: The Natural and Moral History of the Indies (selections)
warum: A Jesuit empiricism before the word: the New World described by observation against the authorities — 'what could I else do then, but laugh at Aristotle's Meteors and his Philosophie'.
quelle: English after Edward Grimston's translation of 1604, as reprinted by the Hakluyt Society (ed. Clements Markham, 2 vols., London 1880; US public domain twice over). Eleven chapters carried, cut to the argument: the Fathers may err on cosmography (I.1, I.9), the burning zone watered and temperate against the ancients (II.6, II.9, II.14), Potosí observed (IV.6–7), and the rationality, writing and reckoning of the Indians defended (VI.1, VI.4, VI.7, VI.8 — the quipus). Grimston's orthography of 1604 is kept as printed. The Spanish original (Seville 1590) is named as source but not yet carried.

titel: The centenary emblem book (eleven emblems, with the Dutch mirror)
warum: The order's self-image at one hundred — engraving, epigram and boast in one volume; the very book its critics mocked. Basis of the planned iconographic path.
quelle: Antwerp: Plantin-Moretus 1640; Internet Archive scans imagoprimisaecul00boll (Latin) and afbeeldinghevand00boll (the Dutch Af-Beeldinghe, verses by Adriaen Poirters), both public domain. Shipped: the engraved title and eleven emblems — one from each of the six books plus three deepenings — as page images with the epigrams transcribed distich by distich, working translations, and each emblem's Dutch mirror page with Poirters's rhymed gloss. The volume's remaining ~110 emblems wait their turn; the iconographic reading path runs through the spine of seven.

warum: Conscience from inside the order against the witch trials: the confessor of the condemned turns witness against the procedure.
quelle: Latin transcribed by eye from the page images of the anonymous first printing (Rinteln: Petrus Lucius, 1631; Internet Archive per_witchcraft-in-europe-and-america_spee-friedrich-von_1631_911, public domain). Shipped complete: Dubium I (the opening question) and Dubium LI (the numbered summa of the trials, pp. 378–392), with this site's working translation (CC0). The torture dubia are the named next step.

warum: The same conscience as poetry: the counter-voice singing.
quelle: German transcribed by eye from the page images of the Cologne print of 1654 (Internet Archive trutz-nachtigall-oder-geistlichs-poetisc, public domain; first published posthumously 1649). Shipped: two celebrated poems complete — the Oelberg lament and the spring 'Liebgesang der Gesponss Jesu' — with this site's working prose translation (CC0). The rest of the ~50 poems wait their turn.

titel: The forged 'secret instructions' of the Society
warum: A forgery that forced a debate — carried as the debate, not as truth.
quelle: Kraków 1614 (Zahorowski). Carried from the bilingual printing of 1857: W. C. Brownlee, Secret Instructions of the Jesuits (New York, American and Foreign Christian Union; Internet Archive instructiosecret00browrich, public domain) — Latin and English on facing pages, chapter and article numbering as the alignment grid; OCR repaired against the page images, all 145 articles bilingual.

warum: The most brilliant attack the Society ever received: casuistry examined by a genius with a grudge and a printing press.
quelle: M'Crie's translation of 1856 (Robert Carter & Brothers), via Project Gutenberg #73959, public domain; Letters V, VII and X complete. French original: the Vallée transcription on fr.wikisource — not yet carried.

titel: Dominus ac Redemptor — the brief of suppression
warum: The corpus's intended closing text: the document that dissolved the old Society. The apparatus ends, deliberately, in 1773.
quelle: Latin after Augustin Theiner, Clementis XIV. Pont. Max. Epistolae et Brevia (Paris, 1852), doc. CCCXVII, whose paragraph numbering (1–41) is carried as the citation grid; Internet Archive clementisxivpon00clemgoog, public domain, OCR emended against the page images. English: this site's unofficial working translation, made directly from the Latin — no full public-domain English translation exists (Nicolini 1854 translates only the restoration brief of 1814).
